html:
An earthquake of magnitude 7.8 that struck the Hawke's Bay region of New Zealand at 10:47 in the morning on 3 February 1931, killing 256 people. It is still the deadliest natural disaster in New Zealand's history.

The shaking lasted about two and a half minutes. In the towns of Napier and Hastings, brick buildings collapsed onto streets and shoppers, and fires broke out in Napier that burned much of its centre, since the water mains had burst. The ground around Napier rose by up to about 2.7 metres, and a lagoon to the north drained, turning some 40 square kilometres of seabed into dry land, where the airport stands today.

Napier was rebuilt quickly, during the Great Depression, in the styles of the day, and is now known for its Art Deco streets. The disaster led to New Zealand's first national building code for earthquakes. Compare the Tarawera eruption of 1886. See New Zealand.
